latin: Vir quidam, caedis<sup>1</sup> accusatus, in judicium vocatus est.
Praeses<sup>2</sup>. — Amicus quem colebas in cubiculo tuo mortuus inventus est. Tu solus eum interficere potuisti*.

Patronus. — Domne Praeses, hoc sine ullo indicio<sup>3</sup> affirmavisti. Nullum est in cadavere<sup>4</sup> vestigium. Nec manuballistae ictu<sup>5</sup>, nec pugione<sup>6</sup>, nec strangulatione, nec veneficio<sup>7</sup> interfici<sup>8</sup> potuit*.
Reus. — Omnia vera ego dicere volo*. Eum invitus<sup>9</sup> occidi. Ei fabulam mortiferam narravi.
Praeses. — Quod est istud novissimum mendacium?
Reus. — Non mendacium est, sed, eheu, verum. Auctor sum comicus, et fabulam ita ridiculam<sup>10</sup> excogitavi, ut homines, qui eam audiant, risu emoriantur<sup>11</sup>.
Haec nolens<sup>12</sup>, cum amico meo qui hanc fabulam audire cupiebat, perincommode expertus sum.
Praeses. — Jubeo te hanc fabulam narrare ut, utrum vera an falsa dicas, videamus.
Reus, pavore percussus. — Impossibile est: nolo* iterum innocentes occidere.
Praeses, summa auctoritate. — Officium nostrum est veritatem invenire. Spectatores ex auditorio<sup>13</sup> discedant<sup>14</sup>! Maneant judices, patronus, reus, custodes duo!
Nos sumus homines fortes et graves. Nihil timemus. Reus fabulam narret!
Reus, iterum invitus, fabulam narravit. Paucis post secundis, patronus risu corruit atque inde obiit.
Post temporis momentum judices obierunt*. Praeses cito in mortem eos secutus est...
Imperturbati tamen manserunt custodes duo... Obierunt* postero die, fabulam enim tardius intellexerunt!
english: A man accused of murder was [brought to] (called into) court.
The president. — The friend whom [you used to frequent] (you cultivated) was found dead in your room. You alone could have killed him.

The lawyer. — Mr President, you affirm this without any proof (cela sans aucune preuve as affirmé). There is no trace on the corpse. He could not have been killed either by a pistol shot, or with a dagger, or by strangulation, or by poisoning.
The accused. — I want to tell the whole truth. I killed him in spite of myself. I told him the story that kills.
Pres. — What is this latest lie?
Acc. — It is not a lie, but, alas, the truth. I am a comic author and I have imagined a story so funny that the people who listen to it die [of laughing] (by laughter).
This, [I] involuntarily, with [my] friend who wanted to hear this story, [discovered] (very unfortunately).
Pres. — I order you to tell this story so that we may see whether you are telling [true or false] (true or false things).
Acc., struck with fear. — It is impossible: I don't want to kill innocent people once again.

Pres., with the greatest authority. — Our job is to find the truth. Let the public (spectators) [leave] the room (of audience). Let the judges, the lawyer, the accused and two [gendarmes] (guards) remain!
We are courageous and serious people; we fear nothing. Let the accused tell the story!
The accused, once again in spite of himself, told the story. A few seconds after, the lawyer collapsed with laughter and died of it.
A [moment of time] after, the judges died. The president followed them rapidly in death...
However the two gendarmes remained [impassive]... They died the next day, for [they took longer to understand] (story in effect more slowly understood)!

footnotes: Caedes, -is, f., murder; caedo, -is, -ere, cecidi, caesum, to cut, to fell. Mortiferus, -a, -um (from mortem ferre), which brings death.
Ictus, -us, m., blow, wound. Manuballista, -ae, f., lit. hand ballista; the ballista was an instrument intended to launch projectiles (cf. ballistics).
Veneficium, -ii, n., poisoning; we have already seen venenum (L. 57, N. 13). The suffix ficium, which is also found in beneficium, comes from facere.
Interficere, to kill; compound of facere (cf. L. 57, N. 14).
Invitus, -a, -um, adj., forced, in spite of oneself.
Ridiculus, -a, -um, which provokes laughter, risible, and not necessarily ridiculous.
Emorior = ex + morior, -eris, -i, mortuus sum, to die.
Nolens: present participle of nolo*. Volens nolens, whether he (she, one) wants it or not.
Auditorium, -ii, n. (from audire, to listen), designates, in a single word, the courtroom.
Discedo, -is, -ere, cessi, cessum, to go away, to move away. Another compound of cedo, -is, -ere, cessi, cessum, to walk.
comments: Syngrapha, -ae, f., note by which one undertakes to pay a sum (Greek origin).

Note a few indefinite adverbs of place which we did not see during our last revision:
Question:
ubi? — ubivis, no matter where (where you want).
quo? — quoquoversus, (towards) all directions.
unde? — undique, from all sides. (Did you notice the demonstrative inde in P. 12 of the lesson and the relative unde in P. 11 of the exercise?)
qua? — qualibet, by no matter what place (by where it pleases).

You could form others in the same way, ubilibet, ubique, quovis, etc. But do not try for the moment to make a complete inventory of them: you will have time to meet them in the course of your reading.

latin: Spectatorum turba in tribunalis auditorium intrat.
Spectatores terrore perturbati quoquoversus fugiunt.
Unde veniunt hi spectatores? — Undique.
Qua iter fecerunt? — Qualibet.
Ubi sedent? — Ubivis.
Potesne ei aliquantum pecuniae commodare?
Quid! In difficultate nummaria est?
Currum sumptuosum non praesentibus nummis emit.
Occasionem se arripere credebat mirificam.
Tribus post diebus in curru reficiendo nummorum mille impensas faciebat.
Nunc nihil habet unde syngraphas solvere possit*.
Pecuniae imperare oportet*, non servire.
english: The crowd of spectators enters the courtroom.
The spectators, troubled by fear, flee in all directions.
Where do these spectators come from? — From all sides.
Which way did they pass (road have they made)? — By any way at all.
Where do they sit? — Anywhere.
Can you lend him some money?
What! He's in financial difficulty?
[He has bought] a luxury car [on credit] (money not present has bought).
He thought he had seized a magnificent opportunity.
Three days after, to repair the car, [it cost him 1,000 francs] (of money thousand expenses he was making).
Now he has nothing [to] (from where) pay his bills (that he might).
One must command money, not serve it = money is a bad master and a good servant.
